headline: Indian Immigrants Have Founded 96 US Billion-Dollar Startups — More Than Any Other Country
subheadline: A comprehensive NFAP study of all 775 American unicorns finds India far ahead of Israel, the UK and China in producing immigrant founders, even as US immigration policy tightens.
body:
• Indian immigrants have founded or co-founded 96 US billion-dollar startups — more than any other country, according to a new NFAP study of all 775 American unicorns.
  • Immigrants collectively built 59% of US unicorns, up from 55% in 2018, with a combined valuation of approximately $5 trillion.
  • At least 76 of the 96 Indian-origin founders first entered the US as international students, mostly from the IITs — a pipeline now under direct threat.
  • The data lands as H-1B registrations drop 38.5%, Congress passes a remittance tax, and DHS moves to end flexible student visa terms.

Indian-born entrepreneurs have founded or co-founded 96 privately held US companies valued at $1 billion or more — more than immigrants from any other country, and by a wide margin. The finding comes from a National Foundation for American Policy study of all 775 American unicorns as of April 2026, which places India ahead of Israel (60), the United Kingdom (47), China (41), Canada (30), Russia (23) and France (21).

A $5 Trillion Immigrant Economy

Across all countries of origin, immigrants have founded or co-founded 455 of the 775 US unicorns — 59% of the total, up from 55% in NFAP's 2018 and 2022 reports. When children of immigrants are included, the share rises to 66%. Nearly 80% of all US billion-dollar startups have either an immigrant founder or an immigrant in a key leadership role.

The collective valuation of those 455 companies: approximately $5 trillion, more than the entire stock market capitalisation of the United Kingdom or Germany. Immigrant entrepreneurs behind US unicorns hail from 76 different countries.

The IIT-to-Unicorn Pipeline

What connects most of India's 96 unicorn founders is their pathway into the country. At least 76 first arrived as international students, overwhelmingly from the Indian Institutes of Technology. IIT Delhi alone has produced 16 unicorn founders; IIT Bombay, 14. The route is well-worn: an IIT degree, a US graduate programme, a stint at a tech firm, then a startup.

Of approximately five million Indian immigrants in the United States, roughly one in every 50,000 has founded a billion-dollar company.

The Names Behind the Numbers

The highest-valued US unicorn with an Indian-born founder is Perplexity, the AI search company built by Aravind Srinivas, valued at $20 billion. Six Indian-origin entrepreneurs have founded two or more billion-dollar companies: Mohit Aron (Nutanix, Cohesity), Jyoti Bansal (AppDynamics, Harness), Ashutosh Garg (Bloomreach, Eightfold.ai), Arvind Jain (Rubrik, Glean), Sachin Nayyar (Securonix, Saviynt) and Ajeet Singh (Nutanix, ThoughtSpot). Jay Chaudhry of Zscaler leads Indian-born founders in personal wealth at $13.1 billion.

A ceiling is visible. The largest US unicorns — SpaceX ($1.5 trillion), Anthropic ($965 billion), OpenAI ($852 billion) — were not founded by Indians. Most of the 96 Indian-founded startups are valued below $10 billion. India leads in volume; it has not yet produced a trillion-dollar company.

"India has sent 96 people to America who started billion-dollar companies. No one else is even close. Almost one in 50,000 of them is a unicorn founder."
— Richard Hanania, political commentator

Uncomfortable Timing

The study lands at a fraught moment. H-1B visa registrations for the 2026–2027 cycle dropped 38.5% from the previous year. The Brookings Institution reported that 2025 was the first year of net negative migration to the United States in half a century. On July 16, the Department of Homeland Security published a rule ending the longstanding "duration of status" framework for international students — replacing open-ended stays with fixed admission periods that add friction to the exact pipeline that produced these 96 companies.

Congress has also passed a 1% remittance tax through the "Big Beautiful Bill." A federal judge recently struck down the administration's attempt to impose a $100,000 fee on H-1B applications.

Stuart Anderson, NFAP's executive director and the study's author, has argued the point for years: immigrant-founded companies generate tax revenue, create entire industries and employ hundreds of thousands of Americans. The 455 immigrant-founded unicorns average 833 jobs each.

"The companies will either struggle because they won't have the talent, or they will have to get creative and find alternate solutions."
— Tahmina Watson Goldman, immigration attorney

What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indian Americans, the 96-unicorn figure marks a generational shift. Earlier waves of Indian immigration gravitated toward stable employment in medicine, engineering and academia. The founders in the NFAP report are overwhelmingly products of the past decade — a cohort that arrived on student visas, built careers in tech, and struck out on their own.

Whether the United States remains the destination of choice is now an open question. As Indian industrialist Anand Mahindra noted: "Despite the challenges, Indian Americans will remain as entrepreneurial as ever. But the new stage will be right here within India, where the startup boom has only just begun."

The data says the door has been extraordinarily productive. The policy direction suggests it is narrowing.
diaspora_angle: 96 Indian-origin founders — most of whom arrived on student visas from the IITs — have built billion-dollar US companies, representing a generational shift from stable employment to high-risk entrepreneurship. The finding coincides with tightening US immigration policy, raising questions about whether this pipeline will remain viable.
